subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Great Permian Extinction
description: A quick win: understand The Great Permian Extinction.

hook.text: 252 million years ago, 96% of marine species vanished. It was the worst extinction ever.

buildup.text: Massive volcanic eruptions in Siberia pumped CO₂ into the atmosphere for thousands of years.

discovery.text: Oceans warmed, acidified, and lost oxygen. Most marine life suffocated or dissolved.

twist.text: The parallels to modern climate change are disturbing — CO₂ rise, warming, acidification.

climax.text: Life took 10 million years to fully recover from the Great Dying.

punchline.text: Earth survived. But 96% of what lived on it didn't.

details.summary: The Permian extinction 252 million years ago was the most devastating in Earth's history, killing over 90 percent of marine and 70 percent of land species. It was driven by massive volcanic eruptions in Siberia that triggered extreme warming, ocean acidification, and anoxia.
details.whyItMatters: The Permian extinction reveals what happens when CO2 and temperatures spike rapidly. Its parallels to modern emissions make it a warning from deep time.
takeaways: Over 90 percent of marine species perished in the Great Dying
Siberian volcanic eruptions released enormous CO2 and methane
Recovery took roughly 10 million years for ecosystems to diversify again

faq.question: What caused temperatures to spike during the Permian extinction?
faq.answer: Eruptions of the Siberian Traps released vast quantities of CO2 and triggered methane release from seafloor sediments. Global temperatures rose 5 to 10 degrees Celsius, creating lethal heat stress on land and devastating ocean chemistry.

faq.question: Why is the Permian extinction relevant to today?
faq.answer: The Permian shows what rapid CO2 increases do to life. Although current emissions are not yet at Siberian Traps levels, the speed of modern carbon release is comparable, raising concerns about crossing similar tipping points.
